report:
## Conclusion: You're right — the best current evidence does not support ivermectin lowering COVID-19 mortality.

**Large, well-designed randomized trials show no mortality benefit.**

The TOGETHER trial (Reis et al., NEJM 2022), a rigorous multi-arm platform RCT in Brazil, tested ivermectin in outpatients with early COVID-19 and found no significant reduction in hospitalization or death compared to placebo. This was one of the largest and most methodologically robust ivermectin trials to date (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869).

The ACTIV-6 platform trial (JAMA, 2023), a U.S. government-funded decentralized RCT, similarly tested ivermectin — including a higher-dose arm (600 μg/kg) — against placebo in mild-to-moderate outpatient COVID-19. It found no meaningful improvement in time to recovery, and the authors explicitly concluded findings "do not support the use of ivermectin" (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801827).

A synthesis of the broader trial landscape notes that over 60 ivermectin RCTs have been registered, with results reported for roughly 31; taken together, the higher-quality, larger trials and updated meta-analyses find no convincing benefit on mortality, hospitalization, or other major clinical endpoints (https://factually.co/fact-checks/health/ivermectin-covid-19-randomized-trials-meta-analyses-efficacy-safety-limitations-87d1c4).

**On the other side:** Some earlier, smaller meta-analyses (often pooling lower-quality or since-retracted studies) reported apparent mortality reductions, which fueled public interest in ivermectin. However, as trial quality improved and larger, pre-registered RCTs were completed, these apparent benefits disappeared — a pattern consistent with early positive signals from small/flawed studies being overturned by more definitive research.

**Bottom line:** The weight of high-quality randomized evidence indicates ivermectin does not reduce COVID-19 mortality, aligning with your stated view.
